processing: Flowers are gathered in batches and dried in shade or over gentle heat, or fumigated or steamed and then sun-dried, as allowed for medicinal chrysanthemum in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia.
harvest_season: Medicinal chrysanthemum is gathered in batches at full bloom, generally from September to November; Boju's flowering ends in early to mid November.
appearance_dry: Loose, somewhat scattered pale flower heads whose petals shed easily.
appearance_liquor: Clear and pale yellow, as is typical of pale chrysanthemum infusions.
appearance_wet: Soft, loose heads with slim pale petals, often coming apart in the cup.
taste_profile: Slightly bitter on the first sip, with a clean chrysanthemum fragrance; drinkers looking for sweetness usually pick other kinds.

brewing.notes: Water at about 90 to 95 °C suits chrysanthemum generally. Top up the pot as you drink; a little rock sugar softens the bitterness.

vintage_note: Sold after the autumn harvest with no vintage, as a medicinal grade rather than a named tea. Industry standards divide it into selected and ungraded lots. As with other chrysanthemum, buy the most recent harvest; loose petals are normal here, but a stale or sharp sulphur smell is not.
description:
Boju is the chrysanthemum of Bozhou in northern Anhui, one of the named kinds set apart by origin and processing in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia. It is grouped with Hangju, Gongju and Chuju as one of China's four famous chrysanthemums, though some lists instead speak of five medicinal ones.

Its identity is medicinal first. The pharmacopoeia method allows several drying routes, from shade drying to fumigating or steaming and sun drying, and those choices affect the look and smell of what you buy.

In the cup it is more bitter and less sweet than Huangshan Gongju, which is the more usual pick for everyday drinking. Because the flower head is loose, it falls apart more readily, so a strainer helps.

If you want a daily floral drink, start with something else. If you are curious about the herb-shop side of chrysanthemum, Boju is an instructive comparison. Traditional uses for it include dispersing wind-heat, but those are claims from Chinese medicine rather than proven effects.
history: Boju takes its name from Bozhou, a long-established herb market, and it is one of the few drugs whose Pharmacopoeia name carries the Bo prefix, alongside Boshao, Bohuafen and Bosangpi, according to local sources. Chrysanthemum tea more broadly became popular during the Song dynasty. No dated account of Boju as a separate kind is on record in what is commonly available.
